channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in August after 0.1% in July, taking annual inflation to 3.4%, with core prices up 0.3%; futures-implied odds of a Federal Reserve increase on Wednesday moved to nearly 90% from 72% the day before.
item.description:
The figures come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the odds from the CME FedWatch tool. Core inflation ran at 2.4% year-on-year against headline 3.4%, and the monthly core reading of 0.3% came against an expected 0.2%; Chinatimes reports the headline readings as in line with Dow Jones survey expectations. At the open on 11 September the Dow rose more than 620 points and the S&P 500 1% while the Nasdaq fell 0.65%, and Wall Street ended the session higher. Oil retreated at the end of the week but remained up around 9% across it, on concerns about prolonged supply disruption along Middle East shipping routes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

An inflation print that moves rate expectations by close to eighteen percentage points in a day is doing more work as a signal about the path than about the level, and the path is what bears on financing and on customer investment decisions. The composition is the part worth separating: headline at 3.4% against core at 2.4% leaves room for food and energy to be doing the work, though no source decomposes the print. If energy is the driver, the path is tied to the shipping and pipeline disruption in the first insight rather than to demand — and on that reading a rate increase would be tightening against a cost shock rather than against demand, which would make its duration a function of the conflict. Points that may be worth considering include whether US financing assumptions carry further increases beyond this week, and how much of the current inflation path a plan treats as reversible on an energy de-escalation.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | Chinatimes

item.title: Thailand's plastics giant is treating sustainability rules and carbon regulation as strategic market opportunity rather than just compliance cost, with a major PET recycling investment aimed at brand demand for recycled content.
item.description:
The Nation's account describes the recycling investment as a key pillar of the strategy. It does not give the size of the investment, the capacity involved, the locations, or a timetable.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The strategic claim is more interesting than the investment, because it is a bet on which way regulation runs: a producer positioning to sell recycled content is betting that mandated and voluntary recycled-content targets hold and tighten rather than being relaxed. If that bet is right, recycled PET supply expands and the constraint on brand-owner commitments moves from availability to conversion — where adhesives, inks and coatings compatibility with recycled substrates is the plausible next limiting factor rather than the polymer itself. Points that may be worth considering include whether product compatibility with high recycled-content PET has been established across the relevant range, and how brand-owner recycled-content commitments in the customer base are trending.

The Nation

item.title: The European Union has abandoned a proposed export duty on aluminium scrap to avoid complicating the signature of its free trade agreement with India, and will rely on environmental rules to curb scrap exports instead.
item.description:
The reversal followed internal negotiations and pressure from India, and the EU is targeting December to finalise the trade deal. The Economic Times account does not give the rate that had been proposed, the volumes involved, or which environmental rules Brussels expects to do the work instead.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The two instruments plausibly reach the same material by different routes: a duty would raise the cost of shipping scrap out, while an environmental rule restricts on the basis of how the material is handled. Which rules Brussels intends is not reported, so the practical effect on European scrap availability cannot be read off this. The trade context is the more transferable point: a materials measure was traded away to protect a wider agreement, which is worth noting for other input-specific measures in the same negotiation. Points that may be worth considering include whether recycled aluminium content assumptions for European packaging rest on domestic scrap availability, and which other input measures sit inside the same December deadline.

The Economic Times

item.title: The India-EU trade agreement gives European carmakers an annual quota of 100,000 built-up combustion and non-plug-in hybrid cars rising to 160,000 by year ten, with in-quota duty on the EUR 15,000 to 35,000 band falling from 110% to 35% then 10%.
item.description:
In-quota duty on the EUR 15,000 to 35,000 band falls from 110% to 35% in the first year and to 10% from the fifth; for cars above EUR 35,000 it falls from 66% to 30% then to 10%. Cars priced below EUR 15,000 receive no preferential treatment, and India will also reduce tariffs on EU cars imported beyond the quota. The traffic runs both ways: the EU will admit 250,000 Indian-made passenger cars a year at a concessional 8%, rising to 400,000, covering Indian-origin combustion and hybrid cars priced up to EUR 50,000, with the duty stepping down to 6%, 4%, 2% and then zero by the fifth year. Separately, the European Commission has asked the EU Council for authorisation to sign and conclude the agreement, which would eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96% of EU goods exports and save exporters an estimated EUR 4 billion a year; it still needs European Parliament consent and Indian ratification, and is expected to enter into force in late 2026 or the first half of 2027.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The price bands are the operative design here: excluding cars under EUR 15,000 from preference protects the volume end of the Indian market while opening the segments above it, so the flow this creates is European premium and mid-range models into India rather than European volume production. That matters for where materials are specified, on the assumption that specification for those models is set in Europe. The quota's ten-year escalation also means the effect arrives as a gradient rather than a step, which gives qualification cycles room to follow it. Points that may be worth considering include whether Indian automotive demand forecasts distinguish locally built from imported models, and which European platforms in the preferred price bands already carry qualified content.

New Indian Express | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | The Economic Times

item.title: Levaco Chemicals' managing director warns of growing location problems in Germany — structurally higher energy costs, more volatile raw material markets and denser regulation — as BASF, Evonik and Covestro cut jobs.
item.description:
Levaco produces specialty and process chemicals and is based at Chempark Leverkusen. The Frankfurter Rundschau's argument is about asymmetry rather than about the burden itself: unlike large corporations, smaller firms cannot offset costs across divisions or regions, and large companies have bigger purchasing volumes and can relocate production more flexibly. Geopolitical uncertainty is named as a further strain on supply chains. In Berlin, Plastics Europe Deutschland used an innovation conference to argue that Germany needs the plastics industry's innovative power to position itself as a high-tech location, with companies showing work on sustainable mobility, climate-neutral energy, medical technology, robotics and the circular economy, and the association pressing for new products and technologies to be converted faster into industrial value creation.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The asymmetry point is the one that generalises, because it describes what a sustained cost gap does to an industry's structure rather than to its margins. If the burden falls hardest on firms that cannot arbitrage it across sites, the effect over time is consolidation and a thinner base of small specialty producers — which for a large formulator is a supplier-base question rather than a cost question, and one that shows up as fewer qualified alternatives rather than as a price. The two items also sit in tension worth noting: one association argues the plastics sector is an engine for a high-tech agenda while a specialty chemicals operator describes conditions as deteriorating, and both can be true at once. Points that may be worth considering include which specialty and process chemical suppliers in Germany are single-site firms of this size, and how a thinner domestic supplier base would affect qualification options.

Frankfurter Rundschau | Plastics Europe Deutschland

item.title: Senior officials say Maharashtra will introduce a dedicated Chemical Sector Policy by the end of October, while exploring 2,500 to 5,000-acre chemical parks at Palghar, Raigad and Ratnagiri and planning an INR 10 billion innovation fund.
item.description:
The officials spoke at ASSOCHAM MahaChem 2026 in Mumbai. The stated intent is to build on the state's existing chemical manufacturing base and reinforce its position as a global hub, with the policy said to open opportunities across specialty chemicals, advanced materials, battery materials, electronic chemicals, advanced polymers, bioplastics and other high-value segments. The account does not give the policy's instruments, the timetable for the parks, or the terms on which the fund would invest.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Chemical parks of this size typically turn on shared infrastructure and co-location, though the release describes neither; on that reading the decision they present to a producer is whether to be inside the fence rather than whether to invest in the state at all. The named segments are the tell: specialty chemicals, advanced polymers and electronic chemicals are the higher-value end rather than commodity capacity, which suggests the state is competing for formulation and R&D rather than tonnage. Against that, an end-October policy with no instruments disclosed is an intention, and the three sites are described as under exploration. Points that may be worth considering include whether Indian capacity plans assume greenfield or park co-location, and what the fund's terms would need to be to matter to a foreign investor.

Assocham

item.title: The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 puts tungsten prices up 622% between January 2025 and April 2026, ahead of tantalum at 196%, cobalt at 134% and lithium at 108%, with about 83% of tungsten mine output in China.
item.description:
Chinese export restrictions have added to the pressure on supply chains. Tungsten's melting point above 3,400 degrees Celsius and its density and hardness are what make it wanted where materials face extreme temperature, wear or mechanical stress, across classic industrial applications as well as aviation and defence. A second concentration figure from the same agency runs alongside it: China holds 97% of global production capacity for battery anode materials, a position Wallstreet:online describes as almost complete control, reached while Western buyers focused on cathode metals such as lithium and cobalt — and without graphite from the Far East, it says, nearly every Western battery factory would currently stand still.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The two figures describe the same vulnerability at different points of the curve. Tungsten shows what a price does when supply is concentrated and the holder restricts exports; the anode number shows a concentration of comparable degree, and today's sources do not say whether export restrictions have been applied to it. For a chemical producer the direct exposure is limited unless tungsten-based tooling or battery-facing formulations are in scope, but the indirect exposure runs through customers — a battery plant that cannot obtain graphite does not consume the materials specified into it either. The 622% figure also sets a rough upper bound on what a concentrated critical mineral can do inside fifteen months, which is a useful reference for other inputs with similar concentration. Points that may be worth considering include which purchased inputs have a single-country share above 80%, and whether battery-facing volume assumptions carry a graphite availability condition.

Wallstreet:online | Wallstreet:online

item.title: The European Commission is extending the digital product passport beyond battery makers, where it began in July, to textiles and furniture, with no piece of furniture saleable without one from 2030.
item.description:
Jan Kurth, managing director of the associations of the German furniture industry, says the passport offers opportunities as well as risks of over-bureaucratisation. He frames it as facilitating new communication with customers while adding another set of sustainability rules on top of the Supply Chain Act, the Transparency Obligations Directive, the environmental claims rules and the Deforestation Regulation, and says most companies will have to increase staff as a result. The report does not say what data a passport must carry, who verifies it, or when the textile rules take effect.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

If a passport carries composition, origin and recyclability data — the report does not say what it must carry — the obligation would run down the supply chain rather than stopping at the manufacturer, because that data sits with input suppliers rather than the assembler. Furniture may be the sector to watch from an adhesive technologies standpoint if a passport ends up exposing disassembly or recyclability, since bonded panel and laminate construction would put the adhesive inside that question. Kurth's list of four existing regimes is the more telling detail: the burden his members describe is cumulative rather than specific to any one rule. Points that may be worth considering include what composition and recyclability data could be supplied today for furniture-facing products, and whether customers in the 2030 scope have begun asking for it.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The Supreme Court has ordered India's federal government to provide a clear pathway for implementing warning labels on packaged food within 10 days, after a complaint from a health non-profit.
item.description:
The order lands on the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India's proposal of last month for a two-phase programme, beginning with red hexagonal warning labels on products exceeding limits in at least two of three categories — added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Business Recorder sets the order against a wider food-safety crackdown in which regulators have raided eateries nationwide. The reporting does not say what the government has submitted, or whether the 10 days runs from the order or from another date.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A deadline measured in days changes the character of this from a consultation to a schedule, and it is the schedule rather than the threshold that determines how packaging suppliers are affected. A labelling change absorbed over a long phase-in would plausibly sit inside normal artwork cycles; one compressed into a short window would concentrate redesign and plate changes instead. The court has not set the rule, only required a timetable for it, so the variable to watch is the interval the government proposes rather than the nutrient threshold. Points that may be worth considering include whether Indian packaging customers have signalled a changeover window, and what artwork and converting capacity would absorb a compressed one.

Business Recorder

item.title: British Glass has asked Number 10 North, the prime ministerial office in Manchester, to intervene in a dispute over the packaging levy, which charges producers by the weight of waste collected and is expected to raise about GBP 1.6 billion a year.
item.description:
Brewers, the pub industry and cross-party MPs have long pressed for a rethink, arguing that charging by weight gives retailers and other customers a reason to move to plastic. The counter-argument reported is that easing the levy for glass alone could raise prices for other materials. The Financial Times account does not give the current rate, the split of the GBP 1.6 billion across materials, or any indication of when the government will resolve the dispute.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A charge assessed on the weight of waste collected works as a material-selection instrument whatever its stated purpose — which is precisely the complaint those pressing for a rethink make. For a supplier of adhesives and coatings the consequence is not the levy but the substitution it may drive: if glass, plastic and board carry different labelling, closure and lamination requirements, which the source does not address, a shift between them would change what is specified rather than how much. The objection from other sectors is the useful signal here: it indicates the total is being treated as fixed, so relief for glass would be redistributed rather than removed, which makes this a fight over shares of the same GBP 1.6 billion. Points that may be worth considering include which UK packaging customers sit in the formats most exposed to a weight-based charge, and whether product ranges are positioned for a shift in either direction.

The Financial Times

item.title: A notice from the industry ministry and the market regulator requires automakers to pay small and medium-sized suppliers within 30 days of acceptance and no later than 60 days, with cash as the default and statutory interest on late payment.
item.description:
Commercial bills and supply-chain electronic vouchers cannot replace cash where the contract does not specify a payment method. The accompanying circular sets out the surrounding mechanics: a clear and explicit starting point for calculating the accounting period, standardised and faster acceptance work, timely and full payment, compliant and convenient payment methods, advance payment during price negotiations, and the handling of exceptional circumstances. The reporting does not give an effective date, name an enforcement body beyond the two issuing agencies, or say how the small and medium-sized threshold is defined.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Three features make this materially different from a statement of principle. A maximum expressed in days is more readily enforceable than a general instruction; making cash the default appears aimed at the substitution by which a payable is settled in a bill rather than in cash; and statutory interest attaches a price to delay. Together they move the question from whether a carmaker pays to what it costs them not to. The size threshold is the detail that decides who benefits, since a rule written for small and medium-sized suppliers may leave a large materials supplier negotiating on the old terms while its smaller competitors are protected — and it may equally reset the reference point for everyone. Points that may be worth considering include what payment terms and acceptance dating currently apply on Chinese vehicle accounts, and whether the group would fall inside or outside the threshold the notice uses.

China Daily | China Economic Net

item.title: The East-West pipeline, which moves Gulf crude to the Red Sea around the effectively blocked Strait of Hormuz, was shut as a precaution after drone attacks in the Riyadh and Medina regions, putting Saudi exports under further pressure.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung describes the kingdom, the world's largest oil exporter, as squeezed from two directions at once: the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and a growing threat to the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Houthi militia in Yemen. The pipeline was the route around the first of those. The Houthi position has strengthened in parallel: Yahoo reports they have seized the port city of Mocha and advanced down the Red Sea coast to strategic islands, and the Economic Times cites Middle East analyst Fawaz Gerges describing their capture of strategic islands near Bab el-Mandab as a game changer that gives them far greater leverage over Saudi Arabia, the Gulf, the United States and global trade. The attacks continued on 13 September, when a vessel was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire and was evacuated according to UKMTO, and Iran said one person was killed and four crew wounded on an Iranian commercial vessel struck off its coast. On price the accounts differ and are worth separating: crude passed USD 100 for the first time since July, the Hindu Business Line puts crude up 44% to USD 104.60 since the war began, and Lianhe Zaobao reports Brent futures hitting USD 110 — while MarketScreener has oil retreating at the end of the week, still up around 9% across it. The Hindu Business Line adds the refining measure: the US crack spread is up 86% to USD 62 a barrel since the war began.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The refining margin is worth carrying forward alongside the crude price. Crude is up 44% to USD 104.60 and the US crack spread up 86% to USD 62, so both the barrel and the refining margin have moved; the two percentages are not comparable, because one measures a price level and the other a margin, and in dollar terms the moves are of similar size — roughly USD 32 a barrel on crude against USD 29 on the crack. Refined streams rather than crude are typically the purchased input here, which is why the margin matters as well as the barrel. The pipeline shutdown is the structural point: it was the physical answer to a closed Hormuz, and with both routes impaired the question moves from price to whether cargoes move at all. Points that may be worth considering include which purchased streams price off refined products rather than crude, and whether supply agreements anticipate a route problem rather than only a price one.
